title: The 7 Essential Hook Patterns — Real-World Workflows

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Lesson 7-8 taught you how hooks work mechanically. This lesson teaches you what to BUILD with them. There are seven distinct hook patterns that cover every professional use case — from auto-formatting code to logging AI activity for compliance audits. By the end you'll have a complete hook library tailored to your specific role.

**The 7 hook patterns at a glance:**

| # | Pattern | What it does | Hook type |
|---|---------|-------------|----------|
| 1 | **Reminder** | Injects project-specific context before Claude acts | PreToolUse |
| 2 | **Standards** | Auto-enforces code/document style after edits | PostToolUse |
| 3 | **Protection** | Blocks dangerous operations before they execute | PreToolUse |
| 4 | **Notification** | Alerts you when Claude finishes a long task | Stop |
| 5 | **Memory** | Saves key context so nothing is lost between sessions | PostToolUse / PreCompact |
| 6 | **Audit** | Creates a timestamped log of everything Claude does | PreToolUse / PostToolUse |
| 7 | **Language / Locale** | Enforces language, region, or format preferences | PostToolUse |

You don't need all seven. Pick the two or three that solve your actual friction points.

**Important — how these scripts actually receive tool data.** As established in lesson 7-8, Claude Code does NOT expose tool details as environment variables (the one exception is `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, which is real). Every other value — the tool name, the file path, the session ID — arrives as JSON on your hook command's **stdin**. Every PowerShell script below assumes it starts with this preamble, which reads and parses that JSON into local variables of the same name used in the rest of the script:

```powershell
# Standard preamble — put this at the top of every hook script
$hookInput = [Console]::In.ReadToEnd() | ConvertFrom-Json
$CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME = $hookInput.tool_name
$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT = $hookInput.tool_input | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT_PATH = $hookInput.tool_input.file_path
$CLAUDE_SESSION_ID = $hookInput.session_id
```

For the one-line shell `command` examples (the `npx prettier`/`black` snippets), the same rule applies — there is no `$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT_PATH` shell variable to interpolate. In practice you'd wrap those in a small script that parses stdin the same way (e.g. with `jq -r '.tool_input.file_path'` in bash) rather than referencing a bare environment variable.

## Pattern 5 — Memory Hooks (记忆)

Memory hooks save important context before it's lost — either to a persistent file or to Claude's CLAUDE.md. Two critical moments: after a significant decision (PostToolUse) and before context compaction (PreCompact).

**Auto-capture decisions to a decisions log:**
```powershell
# memory-hook.ps1 (PostToolUse on Write)
$file = $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT_PATH
$timestamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'

# If Claude just wrote a new file, log it
if ($CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME -eq 'Write') {
  $entry = "[$timestamp] Created: $file"
  Add-Content .claude/session-memory.md $entry
}
```

**PreCompact hook — save key context before compression:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreCompact": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "echo ABOUT TO COMPACT: Please write a one-paragraph summary of the key decisions made in this session to .claude/session-summary.md before continuing."
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
This tells Claude to write its own summary before the compression happens — so you don't lose important context.

**Session continuity file** — rebuild context at the start of every session:
```markdown
<!-- .claude/session-memory.md — updated by hooks -->
# Project Memory

## Architecture Decisions
- [2026-06-15] Switched from REST to GraphQL for the user API
- [2026-06-18] Decided to use Prisma instead of raw SQL

## Files Created This Week
- [2026-06-20 09:12] Created: src/api/users.ts
- [2026-06-20 09:18] Created: src/schema/user.graphql
```
Add this file to your CLAUDE.md with: `Always read .claude/session-memory.md at the start of every session.`

## Pattern 6 — Audit Hooks (审查)

Audit hooks create a complete, timestamped record of everything Claude does. For professional and compliance contexts, this is essential — you need to be able to show what AI did, when, and to which files.

**Complete audit log (every tool use):**
```powershell
# audit-hook.ps1 (PreToolUse matcher: ".*")
$timestamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'
$session = $CLAUDE_SESSION_ID
$tool = $CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME
$input = $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT -replace '\n',' ' | Select-String -Pattern '.' | Select-Object -First 1
$logLine = "[$timestamp] SESSION=$session TOOL=$tool INPUT_PREVIEW=$input"
Add-Content ~/.claude/audit.log $logLine
```

**Auto git-commit after every accepted change:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "git add -A && git commit -m 'Claude Code: auto-commit after edit' --quiet 2>/dev/null || true"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
This creates a commit for every change Claude makes — giving you a complete reversible history. Use `git log --oneline` to see every AI action.

**Weekly activity report** (combine with the Stop hook):
```powershell
# weekly-report.ps1
$lastWeek = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')
$entries = Get-Content ~/.claude/audit.log | Where-Object { $_ -gt "[$lastWeek" }
$report = "Claude Code Activity Report ($lastWeek to $(Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd')):\n"
$report += "Total actions: $($entries.Count)\n"
$report += "File writes: $(($entries | Where-Object {$_ -match 'TOOL=Write'}).Count)\n"
$report += "Bash commands: $(($entries | Where-Object {$_ -match 'TOOL=Bash'}).Count)\n"
Write-Output $report
```

## Three Lenses: Which Hooks Matter For Your Role

**Professional AI/Software Engineer**

Your hooks stack:
1. **Standards** — auto-format + lint + type-check after every edit (non-negotiable for shipped code)
2. **Audit** — auto git-commit after every accepted change (complete revision history)
3. **Protection** — block force pushes, production config edits, unguarded SQL deletes
4. **SubagentStop** — aggregate results from parallel agents in multi-agent workflows

Your user-level `~/.claude/settings.json` should carry the notification hook (always alert you when done) and the audit log (always track across projects). Everything else is project-level.

---

**Public Servant / Corporate Professional**

Your hooks stack:
1. **Audit** — comprehensive timestamped log of every AI action for accountability and compliance. Non-negotiable if AI use must be documented.
2. **Protection** — block access to confidential directories, prevent modification of approved policy files, require confirmation before publishing/sending
3. **Reminder** — inject compliance context before every action: "This project handles personal data under Privacy Act 1988. No PII may be written to log files."
4. **Standards** — enforce document naming conventions, required sections, metadata fields

Key distinction: your audit hook should write to a central location accessible to your team or compliance function, not just a local file.

---

**Freelancer / Independent Consultant**

Your hooks stack:
1. **Notification** — always. You bill by output, not by sitting watching Claude. Step away and get notified when Claude finishes a job.
2. **Memory** — per-client `.claude/reminders.txt` injected via reminder hook. Client A uses Vue; Client B prefers React. Never mix them up again.
3. **Audit** — time-tracking: log every session with timestamps for client billing. The audit log IS your timesheet for AI-assisted work.
4. **Protection** — never accidentally commit to the wrong client's repo. Block git pushes unless the remote URL contains an approved client domain.

Bonus: combine your audit log with a weekly summary script to auto-generate an activity report you can include in client invoices.

**Building your personal hook library:** Create a folder at `~/.claude/hooks/` with one `.ps1` script per pattern. Your `~/.claude/settings.json` references these scripts by path. When you start a new project, copy the relevant hooks into the project's `.claude/settings.json`. Your library grows with your experience — every time you solve a new friction point with a hook, add it to the library.

sections.title: Build Your Personal 3-Hook Stack
Workshop A — The Compliance Audit Stack (Public Servant / Corporate)
sections.content:
Build a complete audit stack that documents AI activity for compliance purposes.

**Step 1 — Create the audit log directory:**
```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path ~/.claude/audit
```

**Step 2 — Write `~/.claude/hooks/audit-full.ps1`:**
```powershell
# Full compliance audit log
$timestamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'
$date = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'
$logFile = "$HOME/.claude/audit/claude-$date.log"
$session = $CLAUDE_SESSION_ID ?? 'unknown'
$tool = $CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME ?? 'unknown'
$project = $env:CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR ?? 'unknown'

# Truncate input to first 200 chars for log readability
$inputPreview = ($CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT ?? '') -replace '\s+', ' '
if ($inputPreview.Length -gt 200) { $inputPreview = $inputPreview.Substring(0, 200) + '...' }

$logEntry = "[$timestamp] SESSION=$session PROJECT=$([System.IO.Path]::GetFileName($project)) TOOL=$tool INPUT=$inputPreview"
Add-Content $logFile $logEntry
```

**Step 3 — Add a weekly summary script `~/.claude/hooks/weekly-summary.ps1`:**
```powershell
$startDate = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')
$endDate = (Get-Date).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')
$auditDir = "$HOME/.claude/audit"
$allLogs = Get-ChildItem $auditDir -Filter '*.log' | Where-Object { $_.BaseName -ge $startDate }
$allEntries = $allLogs | Get-Content

Write-Output "\n=== CLAUDE CODE WEEKLY ACTIVITY REPORT ==="
Write-Output "Period: $startDate to $endDate"
Write-Output "Total AI actions: $($allEntries.Count)"
Write-Output "Write operations: $(($allEntries | Select-String 'TOOL=Write').Count)"
Write-Output "Edit operations: $(($allEntries | Select-String 'TOOL=Edit').Count)"
Write-Output "Bash commands: $(($allEntries | Select-String 'TOOL=Bash').Count)"
Write-Output "Sessions: $(($allEntries | Select-String 'SESSION=' | ForEach-Object { ($_ -match 'SESSION=(\S+)') ? $Matches[1] : $_ } | Sort-Object -Unique).Count)"
Write-Output "=========================================\n"
```

**Step 4 — Wire into `~/.claude/settings.json` and test:**
Run a Claude Code session with several edits. Then run:
```powershell
powershell -File ~/.claude/hooks/weekly-summary.ps1
```
You should see a formatted activity report.

**Step 5 — Schedule the weekly report** (optional):
```powershell
$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'powershell' -Argument '-File ~/.claude/hooks/weekly-summary.ps1'
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Monday -At '09:00'
Register-ScheduledTask -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -TaskName 'ClaudeWeeklyReport'
```

**Outcome:** A compliance-grade audit trail that automatically tracks AI activity and generates weekly reports.

sections.title: Workshop B — The Freelancer Notification + Client-Switch Stack

sections.question: A protection hook detects a dangerous command and writes 'BLOCKED: This operation is not allowed' to stdout, then exits with code 0. What happens?
options: The tool use is blocked — Claude Code stops
The tool use proceeds — exit code 0 means success, so Claude Code continues. The message appears as context but does NOT block the action
The hook is ignored because it wrote to stdout
sections.explanation: Exit code is the blocking signal, not stdout. Exit code 0 = success = Claude Code proceeds. Exit code 1 (or any non-zero) = failure = Claude Code does NOT proceed. Stdout output from a hook is fed to Claude as additional context, but it doesn't prevent execution. To actually block, your protection hook MUST exit 1. Writing a warning message while exiting 0 just informs Claude — it doesn't stop it.

sections.question: You want a hook that applies your company's code standards to EVERY project without having to configure each project individually. Where should you put this hook?
options: In `~/.claude/settings.json` in your home directory — user-level hooks apply to all projects automatically
Hooks cannot be made global — they must be per-project
sections.explanation: User-level hooks in `~/.claude/settings.json` (your home directory) load automatically in every Claude Code session, regardless of which project you're working in. This is the right place for universal habits: formatting, notifications, and audit logging that should apply everywhere. Project-level hooks (`.claude/settings.json` inside a project) override or supplement user-level hooks for that specific project. Both load simultaneously.

sections.question: A freelancer has client A (British English, React) and client B (American English, Vue). How should they set up hooks to prevent Claude from mixing up the two contexts?
options: Put all context in one big CLAUDE.md with both client's preferences
Use a PreToolUse reminder hook that reads a per-project `.claude/reminders.txt` file — each client project has its own reminders file with client-specific context
Rely on memory and manually remind Claude at the start of each session
Use separate Claude Code installations for each client
sections.explanation: The per-project reminders.txt pattern solves this cleanly: each client project has a `.claude/reminders.txt` with client-specific context (language, stack, constraints). A single reminder hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` reads whichever file exists in the current project directory. Client A's project has British English rules; Client B's has American English rules. Claude always reads the right client's context because the hook reads from the current project directory, which changes when you switch clients.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 7-13.** You now have a complete hook pattern library — 7 categories, working code examples, and configurations tailored to three professional roles. Your next step is Part 20 (Building Custom AI Skills) — where you package multi-step workflows into reusable slash commands, which combine naturally with hooks to create fully automated Claude Code pipelines.
